source: Original KaiSip study notes written from the public law (the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the U.S. Code and SEC rules and releases), organized by KaiSip's CSOE blueprint. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the Sarbanes Oxley Compliance Professionals Association (SOXCPA), the SEC or the PCAOB.
overview: This domain covers what Titles III and IV of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act ask of a public company's leaders: an independent audit committee, officer certifications under Sections 302 and 906, limits on influencing auditors and on insider dealings, and wider disclosure. Its center is Section 404, management's yearly assessment of internal control over financial reporting, and the deficiency rules behind it.
analogy: Think of a ship's voyage log. The captain and first mate sign each entry and answer personally if it is false (Sections 302 and 906). An independent inspector, hired by the owners' committee and not by the crew, checks the log (Section 301). Once a year the crew reports whether its safety checks work, and for larger ships an outside surveyor confirms it (Section 404). Crew members may not borrow from the ship's purse or sell cargo while passengers are locked out of theirs (Sections 402 and 306).

topics.overview: Section 301 makes the audit committee of a listed company the independent body that hires, pays and oversees the independent auditor and receives complaints about accounting. SEC Rule 10A-3 turns these duties into listing conditions, so a company that fails them can lose its stock exchange listing.
can_do: Decide whether a director is independent enough to sit on the audit committee
Name who appoints, pays and oversees the auditor and who settles reporting disputes with management
Describe the complaint procedures every audit committee must set up

subtopics.name: Audit Committee Independence
subtopics.definition: Audit committee independence means each member is a director who takes no consulting, advisory or other compensatory fee from the company and is not its affiliated person.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Members paid by or tied to management cannot challenge it freely. Under Section 301 and Rule 10A-3, an exchange must refuse to list a company whose committee fails the test.
how_it_works: Each member must be a member of the listed company's board of directors (Rule 10A-3(b)(1)(i)).
Board and committee fees, and fixed retirement pay for prior service, are allowed; any other consulting, advisory or compensatory fee breaks independence.
The fee test covers payments from the company and from any of its subsidiaries.
Indirect acceptance includes fees paid to a member's spouse or minor child, or to a firm where the member is a partner and that firm advises the company.
A newly listed company gets a phase-in: all but one member may be exempt for 90 days, and a minority for one year (Rule 10A-3(b)(1)(iv)(A)).
subtopics.example: Harbor Point Foods, a listed grocer, invites director Lena Ortiz onto its audit committee. Lena is a partner in a law firm that bills a Harbor Point subsidiary for lease work. The corporate secretary spots the bills in the annual director questionnaire and tells the nominating committee that Lena can join only after the firm's paid work ends.

review: Compare each member's questionnaire answers with vendor payments to related firms
Trace payments from subsidiaries to firms where members are partners
evidence: Accounts payable report of fees paid to members' firms and family
Signed annual independence questionnaires from each committee member
audit_focus.recommend: Have the governance staff refresh independence checks whenever a member's outside roles change.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides who sits on the audit committee

subtopics.isaca_rule: Independence is a bright-line test, not a judgment: any non-board fee from the company or a subsidiary, taken directly or indirectly, or affiliate status disqualifies the member, whatever the amount or disclosure.

exam_traps.trap: A member who is not a company employee is independent.
exam_traps.why: Rule 10A-3 also bars consulting, advisory and other compensatory fees and affiliate status, so an outside adviser on the payroll of a subsidiary fails.

exam_traps.trap: Disclosing a consulting fee to shareholders cures the independence problem.
exam_traps.why: Disclosure cures nothing here. The listing condition is met only when the member stops taking the fee.

key_terms.definition: Any payment for services other than board and committee service, such as a consulting or advisory retainer.
Someone who controls, is controlled by or is under common control with the company.
A fee paid to a member's close family or to a firm the member helps run that advises the company.

subtopics.memory_aid: Board seat, no side fee, no control link.

subtopics.name: Audit Committee Oversight of the Auditor
subtopics.definition: The audit committee, as a board committee, is directly responsible for appointing, paying, retaining and overseeing the registered public accounting firm that audits the company.
subtopics.why_it_matters: If management hired and paid the auditor, the auditor would answer to the people it audits. Section 301 moves that relationship to independent directors.
how_it_works: The committee appoints, compensates, retains and oversees the audit firm's work (Rule 10A-3(b)(2)).
The audit firm reports directly to the audit committee, not to the CFO or CEO.
The committee resolves disagreements between management and the auditor about financial reporting.
The company must fund the auditor's fees and the committee's advisers at the level the committee decides (Rule 10A-3(b)(5)).
The committee may hire independent counsel and other advisers when it judges them necessary (Rule 10A-3(b)(4)).
subtopics.example: At Bluefin Logistics, the treasurer prefers a cheaper audit firm and drafts an engagement letter signed by the CFO. The general counsel stops the letter and sends the proposal to the audit committee chair, because only the committee can appoint and set fees for the auditor. The committee reviews the bids and makes the choice.

review: Inspect committee minutes for the auditor's appointment and fee approval
Trace fee payments to the audit firm back to committee approvals
evidence: Audit committee resolution appointing the firm and approving its fees
Auditor communications sent to the committee directly, not through management
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee approve every audit engagement letter and fee change before it is signed.
audit_focus.decides: Independent directors on the committee decide; management only funds

subtopics.isaca_rule: When a stem asks who hires, pays, keeps or oversees the independent auditor, or who settles a financial reporting dispute between the auditor and management, the answer is the audit committee.

exam_traps.trap: Management appoints the auditor because it negotiates and pays the bill.
exam_traps.why: Section 301 makes the audit committee directly responsible for appointment and compensation; the company only provides the funding the committee sets.

exam_traps.trap: The audit committee runs the company's internal controls.
exam_traps.why: The committee oversees the auditor and financial reporting. Management designs, runs and assesses internal control over financial reporting.

key_terms.definition: An audit firm registered with the PCAOB, the only kind that may audit a public company.
The contract setting the audit firm's scope, fees and reporting line.

subtopics.name: Complaint Procedures
subtopics.definition: Complaint procedures are the audit committee's required methods for receiving, keeping and handling accounting complaints, including confidential, anonymous concerns raised by employees.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Employees often see accounting problems first but fear reprisal. Section 301 makes the audit committee, not management, own the channel so concerns reach independent directors.
how_it_works: The committee must set procedures to receive, retain and treat complaints about accounting, internal accounting controls or auditing (Rule 10A-3(b)(3)(i)).
The procedures cover complaints the company receives from anyone, inside or outside.
Employees must be able to submit concerns about questionable accounting or auditing confidentially and anonymously (Rule 10A-3(b)(3)(ii)).
The committee designs the procedures; it may use vendors or staff to operate them.
subtopics.example: A warehouse clerk at Cedar Ridge Outfitters suspects inventory counts are being inflated before quarter end. Cedar Ridge's hotline, run by an outside vendor under the audit committee's procedures, accepts the report without a name. The vendor logs it and forwards it to the audit committee chair, who asks the chief audit executive to look into it.

review: Walk a test complaint through intake, logging and committee reporting
Inspect the complaint log for retention and committee follow-up
evidence: Complaint log showing receipt dates, status and committee review
Audit committee-approved complaint procedure document
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee review the complaint log at each meeting and track open items to closure.
audit_focus.decides: Independent directors, not management, direct complaint follow-up

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 301 requires the audit committee to own two things: a process for any accounting complaint the company receives, and a confidential, anonymous route for employees' concerns.

exam_traps.trap: SOX requires an internal audit department to investigate complaints.
exam_traps.why: Section 301 requires procedures set by the audit committee. SOX itself does not require an internal audit function, though a listing rule may.

key_terms.definition: A report made without giving the reporter's name.
Accounting or auditing practices an employee believes may be improper.

subtopics.name: Affiliate Safe Harbor, Cures and Notices
subtopics.definition: Rule 10A-3 enforces audit committee standards through stock exchange listing rules, with a control safe harbor and procedures to report and cure lapses.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A lapse in audit committee independence can cost a company its listing, so who counts as an affiliate, and how lapses are reported and cured, matters.
how_it_works: Exchanges must bar the initial or continued listing of an issuer that fails the audit committee standards (Rule 10A-3(a)(1)).
A holder of 10% or less of each voting class who is not an executive officer is deemed not in control (Rule 10A-3(e)(1), opened 31 Oct 2026).
The issuer must notify the exchange promptly once an executive officer learns of material noncompliance, and gets a chance to cure before delisting (Rule 10A-3(a)(3)-(4)).
Independence lost without fault: with notice, the member may stay until the earlier of the next annual meeting or one year (Rule 10A-3(a)(3), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Relying on that grace period, or on most independence exemptions, must be disclosed in the proxy and annual report (Rule 10A-3(d)).
subtopics.example: Director Priya Shah owns 9% of Crestline Marine's voting stock, holds no officer role and takes only board fees, so the board seats Priya on the audit committee. When a merger later costs another member their independence, Crestline tells its exchange and keeps that member until the next annual meeting, four months away and well inside the one-year limit.

review: Compare members' voting stakes and officer roles with the safe harbor limits
Trace any exchange noncompliance notice to the date an officer learned of the lapse
evidence: Beneficial ownership records for each audit committee member
Correspondence with the exchange about lapses and cures
audit_focus.recommend: Have the governance staff recheck each member's holdings and roles after any merger or large stock purchase.
audit_focus.decides: The board seats members; the exchange decides on delisting

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rule 10A-3 works through listing: a holder of 10% or less who is not an executive officer is deemed not in control; lapses go promptly to the exchange, which offers a cure before delisting.

exam_traps.trap: Any director holding 5% of the voting stock is an affiliated person.
exam_traps.why: The safe harbor deems a holder of 10% or less who is not an executive officer not in control.

exam_traps.trap: A member who loses independence must leave the committee at once.
exam_traps.why: If the cause was outside their control, exchange rules may let them stay, with notice, until the earlier of the next annual meeting or one year.

key_terms.definition: Rule 10A-3's test deeming a small holder who is not an executive officer not in control of the issuer.
Exchange procedures letting a listed company fix an audit committee defect before delisting.

topics.overview: The CEO and CFO personally certify each periodic report twice. Section 302 is a detailed civil certification about the report and the controls behind it; Section 906 is a short criminal certification that the report complies and fairly presents. Telling them apart, and from Section 404, is one of the most tested skills.
can_do: List what the Section 302 certification says and to whom deficiencies and fraud are disclosed
State the two Section 906 penalty tiers and what triggers each
Match a report or statement to Section 302, 404 or 906
Explain what the SEC said about disclosure committees and who stays responsible

subtopics.name: Section 302 Certification
subtopics.definition: The Section 302 certification is the statement the principal executive and financial officers sign in each annual and quarterly report about its accuracy and the controls behind it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It makes the top officers personally answerable for what the report says and for the controls that produce it, so they cannot blame staff for errors they never looked for.
how_it_works: Each officer certifies they reviewed the report and know of no untrue statement or omission of a material fact.
They certify the financial statements fairly present the financial condition and results in all material respects.
They state they are responsible for disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, and have evaluated disclosure controls.
They have disclosed to the auditors and audit committee all significant deficiencies and material weaknesses, and any fraud involving management or key control staff, material or not.
Rule 13a-14(a) requires the certifications as exhibits to Forms 10-K, 10-Q, 20-F and 40-F; no one may sign under a power of attorney (Rule 13a-14(c)).
Whoever holds or acts in those roles at filing signs (Rule 13a-14(a)).
subtopics.example: At Larkspur Health, the CFO, Amira Haddad, learns that a payroll supervisor who approves overtime has been padding a friend's hours. The total is small. Before signing the 10-K certification, Amira tells the external audit partner and the audit committee chair, as the certification requires for fraud by anyone with a significant role in internal control.

review: Inspect sub-certifications from process owners supporting the officers' signatures
Trace deficiencies in the issue log to audit committee briefing materials
evidence: Signed certification exhibits for each Form 10-K and 10-Q
Audit committee minutes recording deficiency and fraud briefings
audit_focus.recommend: Have the CFO run a quarterly sub-certification process that feeds the officers' Section 302 review.
audit_focus.decides: The CEO and CFO decide whether they can sign

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 302 is the civil certification of each annual and quarterly report: review, no material misstatement, fair presentation, control responsibility and evaluation, and disclosure of deficiencies and any insider fraud to the auditors and audit committee.

exam_traps.trap: Only material fraud must be disclosed to the auditors and audit committee.
exam_traps.why: The certification covers any fraud, whether or not material, that involves management or other employees with a significant role in internal control.

exam_traps.trap: The independent auditor performs the Section 302 evaluation of disclosure controls.
exam_traps.why: The signing officers, with management, evaluate disclosure controls. The auditor's separate role is the Section 404(b) attestation.

key_terms.definition: Controls that make sure information required in SEC reports is recorded, processed and reported on time (Rule 13a-15(e)).
The officer who leads financial reporting, usually the CFO; a certifying officer under Sections 302 and 906.

subtopics.name: Section 906 Criminal Certification
subtopics.definition: The Section 906 certification is the CEO and CFO's written statement under 18 U.S.C. 1350 that a periodic report fully complies and fairly presents results.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It attaches criminal liability to the act of signing, so a false certification can mean prison as well as fines.
how_it_works: It accompanies each periodic report that contains financial statements, including annual and quarterly reports.
It certifies two things: full compliance with Section 13(a) or 15(d), and fair presentation of financial condition and results in all material respects.
Knowingly certifying a noncompliant report: fines up to $1 million, prison up to 10 years, or both (18 U.S.C. 1350(c)(1)).
Willfully certifying it: fines up to $5 million, prison up to 20 years, or both (18 U.S.C. 1350(c)(2)).
Rule 13a-14(b) lets the officers furnish one joint statement as an exhibit.
subtopics.example: Before Westbrook Mining files its 10-Q, the CEO, Tomas Reyes, is told that a reserve estimate in the report was knowingly inflated by the operations team. Tomas refuses to sign the 1350 statement until the figure is corrected, because signing a report Tomas knows is noncompliant could bring criminal penalties. The CFO restates the estimate first.

review: Compare each 1350 statement's signers and date with the filed report
Confirm each periodic report with financial statements carries a 1350 exhibit
evidence: Furnished 1350 exhibit for each Form 10-K and 10-Q
Disclosure committee minutes showing open issues resolved before signing
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel brief both certifying officers on the criminal certification before each filing.
audit_focus.decides: Each certifying officer decides personally whether to sign

subtopics.isaca_rule: Criminal penalties attached to signing point to Section 906 (18 U.S.C. 1350). Knowing certification of a noncompliant report: up to $1 million and 10 years. Willful: up to $5 million and 20 years.

exam_traps.trap: Section 302 carries the $5 million and 20-year criminal penalties.
exam_traps.why: Those penalties are in 18 U.S.C. 1350, added by Section 906. Section 302 is a civil certification under SEC rules.

exam_traps.trap: Section 906 requires officers to report deficiencies to the audit committee.
exam_traps.why: That duty is part of the Section 302 certification. The 906 statement covers only compliance and fair presentation.

key_terms.definition: Signing while aware the report does not comply; the lower Section 906 penalty tier.
Signing a report known not to comply, done deliberately; the higher Section 906 penalty tier.
An exhibit provided with a report rather than filed as part of it, as Rule 13a-14(b) provides for 1350 statements.

subtopics.name: Comparing Sections 302, 404 and 906
subtopics.definition: Sections 302, 404 and 906 are three separate SOX duties: two officer certifications of each periodic report and management's annual report on internal control.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many exam traps swap the actor, the report, or the penalty between these three sections. Knowing which section does what makes these items quick to answer.
how_it_works: Section 302: the CEO and CFO certify each annual and quarterly report; civil enforcement.
Section 906: the CEO and CFO certify each periodic report with financial statements; criminal penalties.
Section 404(a): management reports on internal control over financial reporting in the annual report only.
Section 404(b): the registered audit firm attests to management's assessment, for accelerated and large accelerated filers that are not emerging growth companies.
Disclosure controls are evaluated as of each quarter-end (Rule 13a-15(b); foreign private issuers yearly, registered funds within 90 days of filing); ICFR as of fiscal year-end (Rule 13a-15(c)).

rows.label: Which reports
cells: Each periodic report with financial statements

rows.label: What
cells: Detailed certification on accuracy and controls

subtopics.example: The new controller at Sunmesa Solar builds a filing checklist. For each Form 10-Q they list the Section 302 certifications and the 1350 statement; for the Form 10-K they add management's internal control report and, because Sunmesa is a large accelerated filer, the auditor's attestation report. The disclosure committee approves the checklist.

review: Compare the filing checklist with exhibits in recent 10-K and 10-Q filings
Confirm filer status before planning the auditor attestation report
evidence: EDGAR filing index listing certification exhibits for each period
Cover page filer status from the latest Form 10-K
audit_focus.recommend: Have the finance team keep a filing checklist that maps each report to its 302, 404 and 906 items.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the internal control report; the CEO and CFO certify

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask three questions: who signs, which reports, and what penalty. Officers sign 302 and 906 for every periodic report; management reports under 404(a) once a year; the auditor attests under 404(b); 906 is the certification with its own criminal penalties.

exam_traps.trap: Section 404 is a CEO certification.
exam_traps.why: Section 404(a) is management's internal control report, and 404(b) is the audit firm's attestation. The officer certifications are Sections 302 and 906.

key_terms.definition: A recurring Exchange Act report such as Form 10-K or 10-Q.
The audit firm's report on management's internal control assessment under Section 404(b).

subtopics.memory_aid: 302 civil detail, 404 annual control report, 906 criminal signature.

subtopics.name: Disclosure Committees and SOX Teams
subtopics.definition: A disclosure committee is a management group, recommended but not required by the SEC, that weighs materiality and disclosure timing for the officers who certify reports.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The CEO and CFO certify reports they cannot assemble alone. A committee of finance, legal and business leaders brings them what they need, while the officers keep the responsibility.
how_it_works: Release No. 33-8124 (29 Aug 2002, opened 31 Oct 2026) required no particular review procedures but recommended a committee to weigh materiality and disclosure obligations on time.
The committee reports to senior management, including the principal executive and financial officers, who stay responsible for disclosure controls.
Suggested members: the principal accounting officer or controller, the general counsel or a senior disclosure lawyer, the principal risk officer, the investor relations head and business-unit staff.
It is a management committee, not a board committee; the audit committee's separate duties come from Section 301 and Rule 10A-3.
SOX program teams and steering groups for Section 404 testing are a company's own choice; the rules assign duties to officers, management, the audit committee and the auditor.
subtopics.example: At Larkfield Tools, the CFO chairs a disclosure committee with the controller, the general counsel and the head of investor relations. Before the 10-Q, the committee reviews a lawsuit update and decides it needs disclosure. The CFO keeps the minutes as support for the Section 302 certification.

review: Inspect disclosure committee minutes for each quarterly and annual report
Trace open committee items to the final disclosures in each report
evidence: Committee charter naming members and the reporting line to the officers
Minutes recording materiality decisions before each filing
audit_focus.recommend: Have the CFO record the disclosure committee's materiality decisions before each certification is signed.
audit_focus.decides: The CEO and CFO decide; the committee advises them

subtopics.isaca_rule: A disclosure committee is a practice the SEC recommended, not a rule. Whatever committees and teams a company forms, the CEO and CFO still certify, management assesses ICFR and the audit committee oversees the auditor.

exam_traps.trap: SEC rules require every issuer to have a disclosure committee.
exam_traps.why: Release No. 33-8124 recommended one but required no particular procedures; the officers' certification duties apply either way.

exam_traps.trap: The disclosure committee is a board committee, like the audit committee.
exam_traps.why: The SEC described a committee of officers and employees reporting to senior management, not a committee of directors.

key_terms.definition: A management group that weighs materiality and disclosure timing for the officers who certify reports.
A company's own team that plans and tests internal controls for the Section 404 assessment.

subtopics.memory_aid: Recommended, not required: the committee advises, the officers sign.

topics.topic_name: Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods
topics.overview: Sections 303 to 306 deal with officers and directors who abuse their position: misleading the auditor, keeping pay earned on misstated results, staying in office after serious violations, and trading company stock while employees are locked out of their pension accounts.
can_do: Recognize conduct Section 303 makes unlawful and who enforces it civilly
Apply the Section 304 reimbursement rule and tell it from the Rule 10D-1 clawback
Explain the unfitness standard for officer and director bars
Decide whether a trade breaks the Section 306 blackout rule and what follows

subtopics.name: Improper Influence on Audits
subtopics.definition: Section 303 makes it unlawful for an officer or director, or anyone acting under their direction, to fraudulently influence, coerce, manipulate or mislead the company's auditor.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An audit is only as good as the evidence the auditor receives. Pressure or deception from insiders can make misleading financial statements look audited.
how_it_works: It covers officers, directors and any person acting under their direction.
The conduct is any action to fraudulently influence, coerce, manipulate or mislead the independent accountant, including pressing it not to tell the audit committee (Rule 13b2-2(b)(2)).
The purpose element: the action aims to make the financial statements materially misleading.
In civil proceedings, the SEC has exclusive authority to enforce Section 303 (Section 303(b)).
Section 303 adds to other laws; it does not replace them (Section 303(c)).
Section 303 speaks of purpose, but Rule 13b2-2(b), which carries it out, applies if the person knew or should have known the action could make the statements materially misleading.
subtopics.example: At Granite Bay Plastics, the chief operating officer tells a plant manager to hand the auditors a shipping log with backdated entries so a sale lands in the quarter. The plant manager refuses and calls the ethics hotline. The audit committee chair hires outside counsel to investigate the request.

review: Inspect auditor management-representation letters and evidence requests for alterations
Follow hotline reports alleging pressure on the audit team
evidence: Auditor communications to the audit committee about pressure or access limits
Investigation report from counsel engaged by the audit committee
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee ask the audit partner privately at each meeting about pressure or limits from management.
audit_focus.decides: Board committees act on findings; the SEC alone enforces civilly

subtopics.isaca_rule: Misleading, coercing or manipulating the auditor to distort the financial statements is a Section 303 violation, whether an officer acts directly or through staff following their direction.

exam_traps.trap: Only the CEO and CFO are covered by Section 303.
exam_traps.why: It covers any officer or director and anyone acting under their direction, such as a plant manager following an executive's instruction.

exam_traps.trap: Section 303 applies only when the officer intended to defraud.
exam_traps.why: The SEC's Rule 13b2-2(b) reaches an officer who knew or should have known the action could make the statements materially misleading.

key_terms.definition: The independent auditor engaged to audit the company's financial statements.
Pressure someone through threats or force to act against their judgment.

subtopics.name: Forfeiture of Bonuses and Profits
subtopics.definition: Section 304 requires the CEO and CFO to repay certain bonuses, incentive or equity pay and stock-sale profits when misconduct forces an accounting restatement.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Executives should not keep rewards earned on results that misconduct made look better. Section 304 lets the company recover them.
how_it_works: Trigger: the issuer must restate because of material noncompliance, resulting from misconduct, with a financial reporting requirement.
Who repays: the chief executive officer and chief financial officer only.
What: bonuses and incentive-based or equity-based pay received in the 12 months after the misstated document was first issued or filed (Section 304(a)(1)).
Also: profits from selling the company's stock during that same 12 months (Section 304(a)(2)).
The SEC may exempt any person from Section 304 (Section 304(b)).
The trigger is misconduct behind the restatement; the CEO and CFO repay even if someone else committed it (Release No. 33-11126, Section IV.A).

rows.label: Trigger
cells: Restatement correcting an error material to prior statements, or material if left uncorrected now

rows.label: Look-back
cells: 12 months after first issuance or filing
Three completed fiscal years before the restatement date

subtopics.example: Orchard Lane Bank restates two years of results after its loan officers hid bad loans from the credit committee. The board's compensation committee lists the CEO's and CFO's bonuses and stock sales from the 12 months after each misstated report first went public, so the company can seek reimbursement.

review: Trace each misstated report's first public issuance date to the pay window
Compare officers' bonuses and stock sales against that 12-month period
evidence: Payroll and equity plan records of CEO and CFO awards
Form 4 filings showing the officers' stock sales
audit_focus.recommend: Have the compensation committee calculate amounts owed by the CEO and CFO whenever a misconduct restatement occurs.
audit_focus.decides: The board seeks recovery; the SEC can enforce or exempt

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 304: misconduct causes a restatement, so the CEO and CFO repay bonuses, incentive and equity pay, and stock-sale profits from the 12 months after the misstated document was first issued or filed.

exam_traps.trap: Section 304 reaches every executive officer for three years of incentive pay.
exam_traps.why: That describes the listing-standard clawback under Rule 10D-1, which needs no misconduct. Section 304 reaches only the CEO and CFO, for 12 months.

exam_traps.trap: Base salary is forfeited under Section 304.
exam_traps.why: Section 304 covers bonuses, incentive-based or equity-based pay and stock-sale profits, not salary.

key_terms.definition: Reissuing financial statements to correct a material error.
Pay that depends on reaching financial or performance measures.
SEC rule requiring listed issuers to adopt a no-fault policy to recover executive officers' erroneously awarded incentive pay.

subtopics.name: Officer and Director Bars
subtopics.definition: An officer and director bar is an order, by a court or by the SEC itself, barring a securities law violator from serving as a public company's officer or director.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Some people show by their conduct that investors should not trust them to run a public company again. A bar removes them from those roles.
how_it_works: Section 305 lowered the standard for a court bar from substantial unfitness to unfitness.
The change applies to both the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (Section 21(d)(2)) and the Securities Act of 1933 (Section 20(e)).
Courts may bar violators of Exchange Act Section 10(b) or Securities Act Section 17(a)(1) who show unfitness (15 U.S.C. 78u(d)(2), 77t(e)).
Section 305 also lets the SEC seek, and any federal court grant, any equitable relief that benefits investors.
Section 1105 lets the SEC impose such a bar itself in a cease-and-desist proceeding (Exchange Act Section 21C(f)); any bar may be permanent or for a set period.
subtopics.example: After a former chief financial officer of Palmetto Freight is found to have hidden liabilities from investors, the SEC asks the court to bar that person from serving as an officer or director of any public company. The court finds them unfit and grants a ten-year bar. Palmetto's governance team updates its director screening checklist.

review: Confirm candidates against SEC litigation releases and court orders
Inspect director and officer questionnaires for prior bars
evidence: Background check reports covering securities enforcement history
Signed questionnaires disclosing any orders or bars
audit_focus.recommend: Have the nominating committee screen every officer and director candidate for existing bars.
audit_focus.decides: Courts or the SEC impose bars; the nominating committee screens candidates

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 305: courts may bar a person from serving as an officer or director of a public company on a showing of unfitness, lower than the old substantial unfitness test. Section 1105 lets the SEC bar administratively.

exam_traps.trap: The SEC needs to prove substantial unfitness to obtain a bar.
exam_traps.why: Section 305 replaced substantial unfitness with unfitness in both the Securities Act and the Exchange Act, making bars easier to obtain.

key_terms.definition: The court standard for a bar since Section 305, lower than the older substantial unfitness test.
Court remedies other than money damages, such as injunctions or bars.

subtopics.name: Insider Trading During Pension Blackouts
subtopics.definition: Section 306(a) bars directors and executive officers from trading company stock they received through their service during a pension plan blackout that locks out most plan participants.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Executives should not be able to sell while employees are stuck holding the same stock in their retirement accounts.
how_it_works: A blackout is a period of more than 3 consecutive business days when at least 50 percent of individual account plan participants cannot trade company stock (Section 306(a)(4)).
Regularly scheduled restrictions disclosed in advance, and merger-related suspensions, are excluded.
A blackout sale is presumed to involve service-acquired stock unless the insider specifically identifies other shares and uses that identification for tax reporting too (17 CFR 245.101(b)).
Profit belongs to the issuer whatever the intent; if the issuer does not sue within 60 days of a request, a shareholder may, within 2 years (Section 306(a)(2)).
The issuer notifies directors and executive officers within 5 business days of receiving the plan's notice, or 15 calendar days ahead if none arrives (17 CFR 245.104(b)(2)).
The issuer files Form 8-K Item 5.04 by the fourth business day after the plan's notice; participants get 30 days' notice (29 U.S.C. 1021(i)(2)(B)).
subtopics.example: Riverside Textiles switches 401(k) record-keepers, freezing participant trades for eight business days. The corporate secretary emails every director and executive officer, files the required notice with the SEC, and tells the stock plan broker to block any trades in their accounts until the freeze ends.

review: Compare insider trade dates with plan blackout start and end dates
Confirm notices reached directors, executive officers and the SEC on time
evidence: Broker confirmations for insiders' trades during the freeze
Copies of blackout notices with delivery dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the legal department block insider trading windows automatically whenever a plan blackout is scheduled.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides how the issuer pursues recovery

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 306(a) reaches directors and executive officers, not all employees. A trade in stock received through service during a qualifying blackout hands any profit to the issuer, regardless of intent.

exam_traps.trap: All employees are barred from trading during a pension blackout.
exam_traps.why: Section 306(a) restricts directors and executive officers. Other employees are the participants the blackout protects.

exam_traps.trap: A director who meant no harm keeps the profit.
exam_traps.why: The statute makes the profit recoverable by the issuer irrespective of any intention.

key_terms.definition: More than 3 business days when at least half of plan participants cannot trade company stock in their accounts.
A retirement plan, such as a 401(k), with an account for each participant.

topics.overview: Section 307 makes lawyers who represent a public company before the SEC report evidence of serious violations up the company's ladder. Section 308 lets the SEC add civil penalties to funds that repay harmed investors.
can_do: Trace an attorney's report of a material violation up the ladder in order
Explain where a civil penalty can go under the fair funds rule

subtopics.name: Attorney Up-the-Ladder Reporting
subtopics.definition: Up-the-ladder reporting is the SEC rule, required by Section 307, that a company's securities lawyers report evidence of a material violation first to the chief legal officer, then higher.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Lawyers often see problems early. The rule keeps them from looking away and sends the evidence to people who can act.
how_it_works: It applies to attorneys appearing and practicing before the SEC while representing an issuer, in-house or outside.
Step one: report evidence of a material violation to the chief legal officer, or to both the chief legal officer and CEO (17 CFR 205.3(b)(1)).
Step two: if no appropriate response comes in a reasonable time, report to the audit committee, another independent committee or the full board.
If reporting to the chief legal officer would be futile, the attorney may go straight to step two (17 CFR 205.3(b)(4)).
Reporting to an existing qualified legal compliance committee meets the duty, without assessing the response (17 CFR 205.3(c)(1)).
subtopics.example: Jonah Price, in-house counsel at Tidewater Pharma, drafts a press release and finds sales figures that do not match the 10-Q. Jonah reports the evidence to the general counsel. Three weeks pass with no inquiry, so Jonah takes it to the audit committee chair, as the rule's second step allows.

review: Inspect the legal department's log of material violation reports
Trace each logged report to a written response and its date
evidence: Written reports from attorneys and documented responses
Audit committee minutes recording escalated attorney reports
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel document every report, inquiry and response under the up-the-ladder rule.
audit_focus.decides: Counsel leading the legal function decides how to respond

subtopics.isaca_rule: Under Section 307, a lawyer's report of evidence of a material violation goes first to the chief legal officer (or with the CEO), then to the audit committee or board if the response is not appropriate. It is an internal ladder, not a report to the SEC.

exam_traps.trap: The attorney must report evidence straight to the SEC.
exam_traps.why: Section 307 sets an internal ladder: the chief legal officer, alone or with the CEO, first; then the audit committee, another independent committee or the board.

exam_traps.trap: The attorney may skip to the audit committee whenever they choose.
exam_traps.why: Going straight to step two is allowed only when the attorney reasonably believes reporting to the chief legal officer would be futile.

key_terms.definition: A material breach of securities law, fiduciary duty or a similar duty by the company or its agents.
The company's most senior lawyer, often titled general counsel.
An optional committee of independent directors set up in advance to receive attorneys' reports.

subtopics.name: Fair Funds for Investors
subtopics.definition: Fair funds are disgorgement funds or other funds for a violation's victims to which the SEC, under Section 308, can add civil penalties it obtains.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Before Section 308, civil penalties went to the U.S. Treasury rather than to harmed investors. Fair funds let penalties help repay those investors.
how_it_works: Condition: the SEC obtains a civil penalty against a person in a court or administrative action, or the person agrees to one in settlement.
Since Dodd-Frank Section 929B (2010), no disgorgement order is needed; the penalty can join a disgorgement fund or other fund for victims.
The addition happens on the SEC's motion or at its direction (Section 308(a)).
The SEC may also accept gifts and bequests for a disgorgement fund or other fund (Section 308(b)).
subtopics.example: After an enforcement case against a former sales chief of Northgate Telecom, a court orders disgorgement of the executive's trading profits and a civil penalty. The SEC moves to add the penalty to the disgorgement fund, and the fund administrator pays harmed shareholders from both amounts.

review: Compare fund receipts with the amounts the order requires
Confirm the SEC's motion directing the penalty into the fund
evidence: Court or administrative order creating the disgorgement fund
Fund administrator's distribution plan and payment report
audit_focus.recommend: Have the company's counsel track any fair fund distribution affecting its shareholders and inform investor relations.
audit_focus.decides: The SEC, not company management, directs penalties into the fund

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 308, as amended by Dodd-Frank Section 929B: any civil penalty the SEC obtains, by order or settlement, can be directed into a disgorgement fund or other fund for the victims.

exam_traps.trap: Civil penalties always go to the U.S. Treasury.
exam_traps.why: Section 308 lets the SEC add them to a disgorgement fund or other fund for victims, an exception to the Treasury rule.

key_terms.definition: An order to give up profits gained from a violation.
A money penalty imposed in a civil, not criminal, case.

subtopics.name: Subordinate Attorneys and Reporting Out
subtopics.definition: The SEC's Section 307 rules tell a supervised lawyer how to meet the reporting duty, and let any covered lawyer reveal confidences to the SEC in narrow cases.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Junior lawyers often find the evidence first, and some violations continue after internal reports. These rules say who carries the duty and when going outside the company is allowed.
how_it_works: A subordinate attorney works under another lawyer's supervision, other than directly under the chief legal officer, and must comply even when following directions (17 CFR 205.5(a)-(b)).
A subordinate attorney complies by reporting evidence of a material violation to the supervising attorney (17 CFR 205.5(c)).
The supervising attorney then becomes responsible for the up-the-ladder report (17 CFR 205.4(c)).
If the subordinate reasonably believes the supervisor failed to comply, the subordinate may, but need not, take the reporting steps directly (17 CFR 205.5(d)).
An attorney may reveal confidences to the SEC, without consent, as reasonably necessary to prevent a material violation likely to cause substantial financial injury (17 CFR 205.3(d)(2)).
Only the SEC enforces these rules; they create no private right of action (17 CFR 205.7).
subtopics.example: Theo Marsh, a second-year associate at an outside law firm, spots backdated contracts while drafting a client's 10-Q exhibits and tells the supervising partner the same day. The partner reports to the client's general counsel. When the general counsel and the board do nothing, the partner weighs telling the SEC.

review: Inspect the law firm's escalation memos from associates to partners
Trace partner reports to the client legal department's log
evidence: Dated emails from the subordinate attorney to the supervisor
Records of any disclosure made to SEC staff
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel require outside firms to confirm how supervised lawyers' reports reach the company.
audit_focus.decides: Supervising counsel owns the report once a subordinate makes it

subtopics.isaca_rule: A supervised lawyer meets the Section 307 duty by reporting to the supervising lawyer, who then owns the report. Reporting up the ladder is required; revealing confidences to the SEC is permitted, never required.

exam_traps.trap: A junior lawyer must follow the matter until the board responds.
exam_traps.why: A subordinate attorney complies by reporting to the supervising attorney; going further is permitted when the supervisor fails, not required.

exam_traps.trap: An attorney must report to the SEC when the board ignores the evidence.
exam_traps.why: Rule 205.3(d)(2) permits disclosure to the SEC in narrow cases; nothing in the rules requires it.

key_terms.definition: A lawyer working under another lawyer's supervision or direction on a matter before the SEC.
A lawyer who supervises or directs another; the chief legal officer is always one.

topics.topic_name: Periodic report disclosures and insider dealings
topics.overview: Sections 401 to 403 widen what companies must disclose and tighten insider dealings: off-balance-sheet arrangements and pro forma figures, a ban on personal loans to directors and executive officers, and faster reports of insiders' trades.
can_do: Name the disclosures Section 401 adds for off-balance-sheet arrangements and pro forma figures
Decide whether a credit arrangement with a director or executive officer is lawful under Section 402
State the Section 403 deadline for reporting a change in an insider's holdings

subtopics.name: Off-Balance-Sheet and Pro Forma Disclosures
subtopics.definition: Section 401 requires annual and quarterly reports to disclose material off-balance-sheet arrangements, and requires pro forma figures to be not misleading and reconciled to GAAP.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Off-balance-sheet structures and flattering non-GAAP figures hid risk before the Act. Section 401 brings them into view.
how_it_works: Financial reports must reflect all material correcting adjustments the audit firm identifies (Exchange Act Section 13(i)).
Each annual and quarterly report discloses material off-balance-sheet arrangements, including contingent obligations such as guarantees, with unconsolidated entities (Section 13(j)).
Pro forma figures in any filing, press release or public disclosure must not be misleading (Section 401(b)(1)).
Pro forma figures must be reconciled with GAAP financial condition and results (Section 401(b)(2)).
Regulation G: a public non-GAAP measure comes with the most directly comparable GAAP measure and a reconciliation, quantitative for historical measures (17 CFR 244.100(a)).
subtopics.example: Quarry Hill Software's investor relations team drafts an earnings release that leads with adjusted profit excluding stock pay. The controller adds a table reconciling adjusted profit to GAAP net income and removes a line implying the adjusted figure is audited. The disclosure committee signs off.

review: Compare non-GAAP figures in releases with their GAAP reconciliations
Inspect contracts with unconsolidated entities for undisclosed obligations
evidence: Disclosure committee minutes approving each non-GAAP measure
Legal entity list showing unconsolidated entities and guarantees
audit_focus.recommend: Have the disclosure committee review every non-GAAP figure and off-balance-sheet arrangement before release.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides disclosures; the audit committee oversees

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 401: filed statements reflect the auditor's material corrections; material off-balance-sheet arrangements are disclosed in annual and quarterly reports; pro forma and non-GAAP figures are not misleading and are reconciled to GAAP.

exam_traps.trap: Pro forma rules cover only SEC filings.
exam_traps.why: Section 401(b) also reaches press releases and other public disclosures.

exam_traps.trap: An off-balance-sheet guarantee is disclosed only in the annual report, once a loss occurs.
exam_traps.why: Section 13(j) reaches each annual and quarterly report and covers contingent obligations that may have a material future effect.

key_terms.definition: A financial measure presented on an adjusted basis that differs from GAAP.
A transaction or relationship with an unconsolidated entity that can affect the company but is not on its balance sheet.
Generally accepted accounting principles, the accounting rules for U.S. financial statements.

subtopics.name: Personal Loans to Directors and Executive Officers
subtopics.definition: Section 402 makes it unlawful for an issuer, directly or through a subsidiary, to extend, arrange or renew personal loans to its directors or executive officers.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Company loans to insiders were used to enrich them at shareholders' expense. The ban removes that conflict, with narrow exceptions for ordinary consumer credit.
how_it_works: The ban covers extending, maintaining, arranging or renewing credit as a personal loan to a director or executive officer (Exchange Act Section 13(k)).
Loans in place on 30 July 2002 survive only if not materially modified or renewed.
Exception: consumer credit, credit cards and similar credit made in the ordinary course, generally offered to the public, on terms no better than the public gets.
Insider loans by an insured bank that are subject to federal insider lending restrictions are outside the ban (Exchange Act Section 13(k)(3)).
The ban does not reach employees who are neither directors nor executive officers.
subtopics.example: Maple Crest Hotels wants to help its new chief marketing officer relocate. The treasurer proposes a low-interest bridge loan through a subsidiary. The general counsel rejects it as a Section 402 loan and suggests a taxable relocation bonus instead, which the compensation committee approves.

review: Inspect receivables and subsidiary ledgers for balances owed by insiders
Check insiders' credit card accounts for terms better than the public's
evidence: Ledger listing amounts owed by directors and executive officers
Signed insider questionnaires on loans and guarantees
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel approve any credit arrangement involving a director or executive officer in advance.
audit_focus.decides: The board or compensation committee approves insider pay instead

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 402: no personal loans to directors or executive officers, directly, through a subsidiary, or by arranging one. The ordinary-course consumer credit exception needs public availability and terms no better than the public's.

exam_traps.trap: Section 402 bans loans to all employees.
exam_traps.why: It reaches directors and executive officers only.

exam_traps.trap: Arranging a loan from a third-party bank avoids the ban.
exam_traps.why: Arranging an extension of credit is itself prohibited, as is lending through a subsidiary.

key_terms.definition: A president, vice president in charge of a main unit, or other officer with a policy-making role.
The normal, regular business the company does with the public.

subtopics.name: Insider Transaction Reports
subtopics.definition: Section 403 requires directors, officers and owners of more than 10 percent of a registered equity class to report changes in their holdings within two business days.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Investors watch what insiders buy and sell. Fast, electronic reports make that information timely and public.
how_it_works: Who files: directors, officers and beneficial owners of more than 10 percent of a class of registered equity (Exchange Act Section 16(a)(1)).
Since 18 Mar 2026, directors and officers of a foreign private issuer with Section 12-registered equity file too (15 U.S.C. 78p(a)), unless an SEC order exempts them.
SEC orders exempt such insiders covered by a listed home rule: Canada, Chile, EEA, Korea, Switzerland, UK (5 Mar 2026); Australia, India, Singapore (20 May 2026) (Release 34-104931, 34-105517).
Conditions: insiders report under that rule, publicly in English within two business days; officers it omits (Australian officers; Singapore officers except the CEO) still file.
Initial statement within 10 days of becoming an insider (16(a)(2)(B)); changes by the end of the second business day after the trade (16(a)(2)(C)).
Change reports are filed electronically; the SEC and any issuer website post them by the end of the next business day.
subtopics.example: Dana Whitfield joins the board of Coastal Freight on 2 March. Coastal's corporate secretary files Dana's initial ownership statement within 10 days. When Dana later gifts shares to a charity, the secretary reminds Dana that the change report is due within two business days and posts it online the next day.

review: Compare insiders' trade dates with filing dates for each report
Confirm each filed report appears on the company website
evidence: Broker confirmations with execution dates for insider trades
EDGAR filing history for each director and officer
audit_focus.recommend: Have the legal staff pre-clear insider trades so change reports are filed within two business days.
audit_focus.decides: Each director and officer owns their own filing

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 403: a change in an insider's holdings is reported before the end of the second business day after the trade; initial statements come within 10 days of becoming an insider.

exam_traps.trap: Insiders report changes within ten days.
exam_traps.why: Ten days is the deadline for the initial statement. Changes in ownership are due before the end of the second business day after the trade.

exam_traps.trap: Every foreign private issuer insider now files Section 16 reports.
exam_traps.why: Ten percent owners of foreign private issuers stay outside Section 16(a) (Rule 16a-2), and SEC orders exempt some directors and officers.

key_terms.definition: A person with voting or investment power over securities, even if held in another name.
The statement an insider files after a purchase, sale or other change in holdings.

subtopics.name: Non-GAAP Measures in Filings and Spoken Remarks
subtopics.definition: Item 10(e) of Regulation S-K governs non-GAAP measures in SEC filings, while Regulation G governs other public disclosures, including calls and webcasts.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Adjusted figures can flatter results. The rules keep them off the audited statements and make sure readers and listeners can find the GAAP comparison.
how_it_works: In a filing, a non-GAAP measure needs the comparable GAAP measure with equal or greater prominence, a reconciliation and management's reasons for using it (Item 10(e)(1)(i)).
No non-GAAP measure may appear on the face of the GAAP financial statements or in their notes (Item 10(e)(1)(ii)(C)).
Regulation G: a measure spoken on a call or webcast complies if the GAAP information is online then and the presentation says where (Rule 100, Note 1).
Regulation G does not reach a foreign private issuer's measure based on non-U.S. GAAP, disclosed abroad, when its securities are listed outside the United States (Rule 100(c)).
subtopics.example: On Harlow Logistics' quarterly call, the CFO mentions adjusted free cash flow; the investor relations lead has already posted the GAAP comparison online and reads out the page address. For the Form 10-Q, the controller moves the same figure out of the notes and into MD&A, below the GAAP cash flow line.

review: Compare each non-GAAP figure in the 10-K with its placement and GAAP counterpart
Match call scripts against website postings timestamped before the call
evidence: Disclosure committee checklist for non-GAAP measures
Website logs showing when reconciliations were posted
audit_focus.recommend: Have the disclosure committee review every non-GAAP figure before calls, releases and filings.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses the measures; the CFO answers for them

subtopics.isaca_rule: In SEC filings, Item 10(e) keeps non-GAAP measures off the face of the statements and notes and gives GAAP equal prominence; elsewhere, Regulation G applies, including spoken remarks backed by a website posting.

exam_traps.trap: A reconciled non-GAAP line may appear on the face of the income statement.
exam_traps.why: Item 10(e)(1)(ii)(C) bars non-GAAP measures from the face of the GAAP statements and from the notes, reconciled or not.

exam_traps.trap: Regulation G does not reach figures spoken on an earnings call.
exam_traps.why: It covers any public disclosure; Note 1 to Rule 100 explains how a spoken measure complies through a website posting.

key_terms.definition: The Regulation S-K rule for non-GAAP financial measures included in SEC filings.
Showing the comparable GAAP measure at least as prominently as the non-GAAP measure.

topics.overview: Section 404(a) makes management report each year on internal control over financial reporting and assess whether it is effective as of fiscal year-end. Section 404(b) adds an audit firm attestation for larger filers. The deficiency definitions decide what management must disclose and whether it can call controls effective.
can_do: List what management's annual internal control report must contain and its as-of date
Decide whether a filer needs the auditor's attestation report
Classify a deficiency by the reasonable possibility of a material misstatement
Conclude on effectiveness when a material weakness exists or was fixed before year-end

subtopics.name: Management's Internal Control Report
subtopics.definition: Management's internal control report, required by Section 404(a), states management's responsibility for internal control over financial reporting and assesses its effectiveness as of fiscal year-end.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It gives investors management's own conclusion on the controls behind the numbers, made against a recognized framework and backed by evidence.
how_it_works: The report goes in each annual report only; management keeps evidential matter, including documentation, reasonably supporting it (Item 308, Instruction 2).
It states management's responsibility, names the framework used, and gives the assessment as of the end of the most recent fiscal year (Item 308(a)).
The framework must be suitable and recognized, set through due process with public comment (Rule 13a-15(c)); COSO is the usual choice.
SEC guidance describes a top-down, risk-based evaluation that starts from financial reporting risks and entity-level controls (Release No. 33-8810, Section II.A).
Newly public companies skip the report in their first annual report, with a required transition statement (Item 308, Instruction 1).
Each 10-Q and 10-K also discloses any change in ICFR during the last quarter that materially affected, or is reasonably likely to materially affect, ICFR (Item 308(c)).
subtopics.example: Juniper Valley Foods closes its fiscal year on 30 June. Its controller plans the internal control assessment around that date, starting with risks to material accounts and the entity-level controls over them. Management documents its testing so the evidence supports its conclusion as of 30 June.

review: Trace in-scope accounts to financial statement risks and assertions
Inspect management's test results for the year-end as-of date
evidence: Management's risk assessment linking accounts to key controls
Control test workpapers dated near fiscal year-end
audit_focus.recommend: Have management keep scoping, testing and conclusions together in one documented assessment file.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns and signs the year-end conclusion

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 404(a) is management's annual report: responsibility, the framework used, and an effectiveness assessment as of fiscal year-end, backed by evidence.

exam_traps.trap: The assessment covers the whole fiscal year.
exam_traps.why: Management assesses effectiveness as of the end of the most recent fiscal year, a point in time, not the full period.

exam_traps.trap: Management must document every control in every process.
exam_traps.why: Release No. 33-8810 says documentation need not cover every control; it focuses on the controls that address financial reporting risks.

key_terms.definition: A process giving reasonable assurance that financial reporting is reliable and statements follow GAAP (Rule 13a-15(f)).
A recognized control framework set through due process with public comment, such as COSO.
Company-wide controls, such as the control environment and period-end reporting, that affect many accounts.

subtopics.name: Auditor Attestation and Its Exemptions
subtopics.definition: Under Section 404(b), the company's registered audit firm attests to and reports on management's internal control assessment, unless the company is exempt by filer status.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An outside attestation adds independent assurance to management's view, but Congress exempted smaller and newer companies to limit cost.
how_it_works: The audit firm that issues the financial statement audit report attests; it is not a separate engagement (Section 404(b)).
Non-accelerated filers are exempt from 404(b) (Section 404(c), added by Dodd-Frank Section 989G(a)).
Emerging growth companies are exempt while they keep that status (JOBS Act Section 103).
An emerging growth company has total annual gross revenues under $1.235 billion (Rule 12b-2; cap effective 20 Sep 2022, Release No. 33-11098; checked 31 Oct 2026).
It keeps that status at most until the fiscal year-end after its IPO's fifth anniversary, unless revenue, debt issuance or large accelerated filer status ends it sooner (Rule 12b-2).
Exempt companies still file management's Section 404(a) report; Section 405 exempts registered investment companies from Sections 401, 402 and 404.
subtopics.example: Tallgrass Robotics listed its shares three years ago and its revenues remain well under the cap. Its public float has grown past $75 million, making it an accelerated filer, but its CFO tells the audit committee that emerging growth status still lets Tallgrass omit the outside attestation for now.

review: Confirm filer status from the public float and revenue tests
Compare filer status with the reports included in the annual report
evidence: Year-end filer status calculation with second-quarter public float
Engagement letter scope for any internal control attestation
audit_focus.recommend: Have the finance team recompute filer status at each year-end before planning the audit.
audit_focus.decides: Management determines status from the Rule 12b-2 tests

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 404(b) attestation is required only for accelerated and large accelerated filers that are not emerging growth companies. Every annual-report filer past its first annual report still owes management's 404(a) report.

exam_traps.trap: Non-accelerated filers are exempt from all of Section 404.
exam_traps.why: Section 404(c) exempts them only from the auditor attestation in 404(b). Management's 404(a) report is still required.

key_terms.definition: Under Rule 12b-2, generally a filer with public float of $75 million to under $700 million that meets other conditions.
A filer that is neither an accelerated nor a large accelerated filer under Rule 12b-2.
A newer issuer with revenues under the Rule 12b-2 cap, allowed scaled disclosure and exempt from 404(b).

subtopics.name: Deficiency Severity
subtopics.definition: Deficiency severity ranks control gaps as a deficiency, a significant deficiency or a material weakness, by how likely and how large a misstatement they could let through.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Severity decides what management must disclose and whether it can call controls effective, so classifying a deficiency is a key compliance judgment.
how_it_works: Material weakness: a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of annual or interim statements will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis (Rule 12b-2).
Significant deficiency: less severe than a material weakness, yet important enough to merit the attention of those overseeing financial reporting (Rule 12b-2).
Severity depends on whether a misstatement could occur, not on whether one actually did (Release No. 33-8810, Section II.B.1).
Deficiencies affecting the same account or disclosure are considered together; compensating controls count only if precise enough.
Indicators of a material weakness include fraud by senior management and restating prior statements to correct a material misstatement.

rows.label: Severity
cells: A control gap of any size
Merits attention of those overseeing reporting
Reasonable possibility of a material misstatement missed

rows.label: Reported to
cells: Auditors, audit committee and the public

subtopics.example: At Ironwood Chemicals, management finds that access to the vendor master file was never restricted, so buyers could add vendors and approve their invoices. Testing finds no false vendors. The controller still rates the gap by what could happen, weighs compensating controls, and briefs the audit committee.

review: Evaluate each deficiency for likelihood and potential magnitude of misstatement
Check deficiencies for consistent ratings across business units
evidence: Deficiency evaluation matrix with likelihood and magnitude ratings
Compensating control test results showing precision
audit_focus.recommend: Have management document each severity conclusion and report significant deficiencies and material weaknesses to the audit committee.
audit_focus.decides: Management classifies severity; the audit committee oversees

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rate a deficiency by the reasonable possibility and size of a misstatement that could escape prevention or timely detection, not by the errors actually found.

exam_traps.trap: No misstatement occurred, so the deficiency cannot be a material weakness.
exam_traps.why: Severity rests on whether there is a reasonable possibility of a material misstatement, whether or not one actually occurred.

exam_traps.trap: Significant deficiencies must be disclosed in management's annual report.
exam_traps.why: Only material weaknesses must be disclosed there. Significant deficiencies go to the auditors and the audit committee under the Section 302 certification.

key_terms.definition: A control that meets the objective of a failed control well enough to reduce the risk.
A likelihood that is either reasonably possible or probable.

subtopics.name: Concluding on Effectiveness
subtopics.definition: Concluding on effectiveness means management states plainly in its Section 404(a) report whether internal control over financial reporting was effective at fiscal year-end.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A clear conclusion tells investors whether to rely on the controls. Hedged wording or a conclusion that ignores a known material weakness would mislead them.
how_it_works: Management may not conclude that controls are effective if one or more material weaknesses exist at year-end (Item 308(a)(3)).
A material weakness fixed and shown to work before year-end does not stop an effective conclusion (Release No. 33-8810, Section II.A).
Management should not qualify its conclusion, such as effective except for a stated weakness (Release No. 33-8810, Section II.B.2).
Each material weakness is disclosed in management's report (Item 308(a)(3)).
A later restatement does not by itself require management to revise a prior conclusion, though disclosures may need updating.
subtopics.example: At Bayview Instruments, testing in November shows the inventory reserve review failed. A new review begins in December, but there are too few instances to show it works by 31 December. The CFO drafts the 404(a) report stating that internal control was not effective and describing the weakness and the fix in progress.

review: Inspect the year-end deficiency list against the drafted conclusion
Inspect remediation testing for enough operation before year-end
evidence: Remediation test results dated before fiscal year-end
Draft 404(a) report wording reviewed by the disclosure committee
audit_focus.recommend: Have management base the year-end conclusion on remediation evidence and state the conclusion without qualification.
audit_focus.decides: Management makes the conclusion; the audit committee reviews it

subtopics.isaca_rule: A material weakness open at year-end means controls are not effective, with no except-for wording. One fixed and tested before year-end does not block an effective conclusion.

exam_traps.trap: A weakness found at any point in the year means controls were ineffective.
exam_traps.why: The assessment is as of year-end. If the weakness was remediated and tested before then, management may conclude controls are effective.

key_terms.definition: Fixing a control deficiency and showing the fix works.
A conclusion with an exception, such as effective except for one area, which management should not give.

topics.topic_name: Ethics code, financial expert, SEC review and real-time disclosure
topics.overview: Sections 406 to 409 add disclosure duties around governance and timing: whether a company has an ethics code for senior financial officers and an audit committee financial expert (and why not if not), how often the SEC reviews filings, and fast disclosure of material changes.
can_do: Apply the disclose-or-explain rule to the ethics code and the financial expert
State how quickly a change in or waiver of the ethics code must be disclosed
State the minimum frequency of SEC review and what real-time disclosure requires

subtopics.name: Code of Ethics for Senior Financial Officers
subtopics.definition: Section 406 requires each issuer to disclose whether it has a code of ethics for its senior financial officers and, if not, why not.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A code sets expected conduct for the people who prepare the numbers. Disclosure lets investors see whether one exists and when it is bent.
how_it_works: Disclose whether a code covers the principal executive, financial and accounting officers or controller, or explain why not (Item 406(a)); the Act named only the financial officers.
A code is written standards that deter wrongdoing and promote honest conduct, full and fair disclosure, compliance, prompt internal reporting and accountability (Item 406(b)).
Make the code available by filing it, posting it online with the address and posting disclosed in the annual report, or offering free copies on request (Item 406(c)).
Any change in or waiver of the code must be disclosed immediately (Section 406(b)): on Form 8-K within four business days (Item 5.05).
A website posting within four business days can replace the 8-K if the last annual report announced it; foreign private issuers do not file Form 8-K.
subtopics.example: The board of Pinecone Media amends its finance code to let senior finance staff accept supplier gifts up to $100. The general counsel posts the amended code on the investor website the same day, within the four business days allowed, as the company's annual report said it would.

review: Compare board minutes granting waivers with posted or filed disclosures
Confirm the code's availability matches the annual report statement
evidence: Form 8-K filings or website postings of code changes and waivers
Board minutes approving amendments and waivers
audit_focus.recommend: Have the legal department post or file each approved change or waiver on the same day.
audit_focus.decides: The board grants or refuses waivers

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 406 is disclose-or-explain for having the code, and immediate disclosure for any change or waiver affecting senior financial officers.

exam_traps.trap: Section 406 requires every issuer to adopt a code of ethics.
exam_traps.why: It requires disclosure of whether a code exists and, if not, the reason. Listing rules may separately require one.

exam_traps.trap: Waivers can wait for the next annual report.
exam_traps.why: Changes and waivers must be disclosed immediately, by Form 8-K or electronic means.

key_terms.definition: Written standards for honest conduct, fair disclosure and legal compliance by senior financial officers.
Permission to depart from a provision of the code.

subtopics.name: Audit Committee Financial Expert
subtopics.definition: Section 407 requires each issuer to disclose whether its audit committee has at least one financial expert, as the SEC defines it, and if not, why not.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Investors want to know whether the committee overseeing the auditor can understand complex accounting.
how_it_works: The board determines whether at least one member is an audit committee financial expert (Item 407(d)(5)(i)).
If one exists, disclose the name and whether that person is independent.
If none exists, say so and explain why.
Attributes include understanding GAAP, estimates and accruals, comparable financial statement experience, internal control and audit committee functions (Item 407(d)(5)(ii)).
The label makes no one an expert for any purpose, including Securities Act Section 11, and adds no duties or liability (Item 407(d)(5)(iv)).
The attributes may come from a finance or audit post, actively supervising such a person, overseeing financial reporting, or other relevant experience (Item 407(d)(5)(iii)).
subtopics.example: Highland Ferries' board reviews the backgrounds of its audit committee members and finds that the chair, a retired public company controller, has all five attributes. The proxy names the chair as the audit committee financial expert and states that the chair is independent under the exchange's listing standards. The board secretary records the determination in the minutes.

review: Trace the proxy's expert disclosure to the board's documented basis
Compare each designated expert's background with the five attributes
evidence: Board resolution naming the expert and stating independence
Director questionnaires describing accounting and audit experience
audit_focus.recommend: Have the nominating committee track financial expert attributes when planning audit committee succession.
audit_focus.decides: The directors make the call each year, not the nominee

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 407 is disclose-or-explain: name the financial expert and say whether they are independent, or state that there is none and why.

exam_traps.trap: Section 407 requires every audit committee to have a financial expert.
exam_traps.why: It requires disclosure. A company without one must say so and explain why.

exam_traps.trap: The financial expert carries greater liability than other members.
exam_traps.why: Item 407 states the designation imposes no greater duties, obligations or liability.

key_terms.definition: A member the board finds has all five attributes the SEC lists for the role.
A rule requiring a company to state whether it meets a practice and, if not, why.

subtopics.name: SEC Review and Real-Time Disclosure
subtopics.definition: Section 408 requires the SEC to review each reporting issuer's disclosures at least once every three years; Section 409 requires rapid disclosure of material changes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Regular review catches poor disclosure, and real-time disclosure keeps investors from trading on stale information.
how_it_works: The SEC reviews issuers' disclosures, including financial statements, on a regular and systematic basis (Section 408(a)).
No reporting issuer may go more than 3 years without review (Section 408(c)).
Scheduling factors include restatements, stock price volatility, largest market value, price-to-earnings gaps and economic importance (Section 408(b)).
Section 409: issuers disclose material changes in financial condition or operations on a rapid and current basis, in plain English, as SEC rules require.
Form 8-K, the current report, is generally due within four business days after the event (Form 8-K General Instruction B.1).
subtopics.example: Seabright Water receives an SEC comment letter on its revenue note, its first in three years. The CFO drafts responses with the audit committee chair's input and updates the next 10-Q's note. Separately, the disclosure committee uses the SEC's current-report rules to announce a plant closure quickly.

review: Trace SEC comment letters to responses and changes in later filings
Compare dates of material events with their public disclosure dates
evidence: SEC comment letters and company response letters
Current reports filed for material events with event dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the disclosure committee log material events and file current reports within the SEC's deadlines.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides disclosures; the SEC reviews them

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 408 sets a floor of SEC review at least once every three years, with riskier issuers reviewed more often. Section 409 requires rapid, current disclosure of material changes.

exam_traps.trap: The SEC reviews every issuer's filings every year.
exam_traps.why: Section 408 sets a minimum of once every three years; scheduling factors decide which issuers are reviewed more often.

exam_traps.trap: A material agreement can wait for the next Form 10-Q.
exam_traps.why: Section 409 calls for rapid, current disclosure; a Form 8-K is generally due within four business days after the event.

key_terms.definition: The SEC staff's written questions or requests after reviewing a filing.
Prompt public disclosure of material changes, as Section 409 requires.

subtopics.name: Form 8-K Non-Reliance, Furnished Items and the Safe Harbor
subtopics.definition: Form 8-K, the current report behind Section 409, also sets what triggers a non-reliance report, which items are furnished rather than filed, and a narrow antifraud safe harbor.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Restatements, earnings releases and missed reports carry real liability, so the disclosure team must know what starts the clock and what a miss exposes.
how_it_works: Item 4.02(a): report when the board, a board committee or authorized officers conclude previously issued statements should no longer be relied on because of an error.
Item 4.02(b)-(c): if the independent auditor gives notice, the company sends the auditor its disclosure and asks for a letter to the SEC saying whether it agrees.
Items 2.02 and 7.01 are furnished, not deemed filed for Exchange Act Section 18 unless the company says so or incorporates them (General Instruction B.2).
Rule 13a-11(c): missing a report required solely by certain items, Item 1.01 and Item 4.02(a) among them, is not deemed a Rule 10b-5 violation.
The safe harbor leaves the filing duty in Rule 13a-11(a) in place, so a missed report is still a breach.
subtopics.example: A physical count at Brightwater Mills exposes a material prior-year inventory error. That afternoon the board decides the old figures can no longer be trusted, and the disclosure team dates its Form 8-K draft from that decision. Its next earnings release is furnished under Item 2.02.
